newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Statistician mulls reorganising Australia CPI.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Statistician mulls reorganising Australia CPI.

text.p: The Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) is looking at a broad reorganisation of its price measures, consolidating the indexes into an integrated system much like the national accounts gross domestic product (GDP) measures.
The bureau may also adjust its price measures to remove the effects of indirect taxes, seasonality and volatility.
Describing its thoughts in an information paper this week, the bureau has called for comments from users of its statistics.

"There is scope to enhance the analytical value of the information through the ABS drawing the series together and presenting them as a system or family of price indexes," the bureau said in its information paper.
The changes would not, however, happen for perhaps three years or more, a bureau spokesman told Reuters on Tuesday.
Currently the bureau produces a mixed bag of price indexes which do not integrate into a single picture of the economy.

There are price indexes for manufacturing input and output but none for services. Housing and construction are covered specifically but other industries are not. Wages are measured in some ways but not others.
And the most influential of price measures, the consumer price index (CPI), is not matched by either an investment price index or a producer price index.

So the bureau describes in its information paper a Domestic Final Purchases index, measuring the overall price movements for all consumption and investment goods and services at their final points of exchange in the economy -- sale to final users.
That index would be broken down into a Household Consumption Purchases index, similar to and potentially replacing the CPI, and a similar index for investment purchases.
Both would be further divided into different classes of goods or services.
The Household Consumption Purchases index might be published monthly. Australia is one of the few developed countries that publishes its CPI only quarterly.
The information paper discussed a related compilation of indexes that would measure prices at earlier points in the productive process.
Measured at the final step in the productive process before distribution, the system would produce a number something like a producer price index.
These two compilations would appear alongside indexes measuring labour costs and export prices.
Australian economic analysis increasingly focuses on price measures adjusted for misleading irregular effects and the bureau said it could respond with adjusted series.

"In recognition of the increased attention being given to measures of underlying inflation, alternative methods of abstracting from the effects of changes in indirect taxes and subsidies, seasonality and volatility are considered," it said.

"A 'specific adjustment method', involving the development of net price indexes (at constant tax rates) and the application of seasonal adjustment and smoothing techniques, is assessed as being conceptually superior."
Currently, the bureau's price indexes simply reflect the raw state of prices in the economy, which economists say is not always the most useful indicator for analysis.

One of the few concessions to a more processed number is the "Treasury underlying CPI", which is similar to the U.S. core inflation rate. The bureau mentions this underlying number in its CPI release each quarter.
A bureau study in 1991 found that Australian inflation was not notably seasonal. But the spokesman said that the question should be revisited.
The bureau is a strong advocate of trend estimates, which it calculates with Henderson moving averages. It has does not, however, issue trend estimates for its price indexes.
